source.text: Dharmarakṣa, trans. (attributed), Ullambana Sutra (Taishō T685): nearly complete, with a few passages shortened

ur01.heading: A Mother Reborn as a Hungry Ghost
ur01.plain: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at Jeta Grove in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Venerable Maudgalyāyana had just attained the six spiritual powers, and wishing to save his parents and repay the kindness of being nursed and raised, he looked over the world with the eye of the Way. He saw that his late mother had been reborn as a hungry ghost; she never saw food, and was nothing but skin and bone.
ur01.commentary: The first thing Maudgalyāyana, foremost in spiritual powers, did after awakening was to repay his parents' kindness. But his mother was suffering in the realm of hunger (the hungry ghost realm).

ur02.heading: The Rice Turns to Fire
ur02.plain: Grieving, Maudgalyāyana at once filled his bowl with rice and brought it to his mother. When she received it, she covered the bowl with her left hand and with her right formed the rice into a ball to eat, but before it reached her mouth it turned into burning coals, and in the end she could not eat. Maudgalyāyana cried out and wept bitterly, ran to the Buddha and told him everything.
ur02.commentary: She covered the bowl with her left hand for fear that other ghosts would snatch it. The stinginess of not knowing how to give while alive remained after death, and became the result of food turning to fire. Even a son with great spiritual powers could do nothing about his mother's karma.

ur03.heading: By the Power of the Sangha
ur03.plain: The Buddha said: "The roots of your mother's wrongdoing are deeply knotted; your strength alone cannot help her. Even if your filial devotion moves heaven and earth, the gods of heaven and earth, evil māras and outside teachers, Taoist masters and the Four Heavenly Kings can do nothing. Only by the majestic power of the assembled Sangha of the ten directions can she be freed. Now I will tell you the way of rescue, so that all who are in difficulty may leave sorrow and suffering."
ur03.commentary: What one person's devotion and spiritual power cannot do is accomplished by the power of the whole practicing assembly. It teaches that the merit of practicing together is great.

ur04.heading: The Offering on the Fifteenth Day of the Seventh Month
ur04.plain: The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the Sangha of the ten directions holds the pravāraṇā, for the sake of parents of seven generations and present parents who are in difficulty, gather food of a hundred flavors and five kinds of fruit, vessels for drawing water, scented oil and lamps, beds and bedding, the best things of the world, place them in a bowl, and offer them to the virtuous monastics of the ten directions."
ur04.commentary: The fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month is pravāraṇā, when monastics finish the three-month summer retreat and invite one another to point out their faults. The offering is to be made when the merit of monastics just finishing their practice is greatest. This is the origin of Baekjung, the Ullambana festival.

ur05.heading: The Merit of the Offering
ur05.plain: "If offerings are made in this way to the monastics at pravāraṇā, present parents, parents of seven generations and relatives in the six realms will escape the suffering of the three evil paths and be freed on the spot, with clothing and food naturally provided. If someone's parents are living, they will have a hundred years of blessing and happiness; and parents of seven generations who have passed away will be born freely in the heavens and enter the light of heavenly flowers."
ur05.commentary: The Baekjung offering has two meanings: wishing blessings and long life for living parents, and good rebirth for departed ancestors.

ur06.heading: The Mother Freed from Suffering
ur06.plain: Then the Buddha told the Sangha of the ten directions first to make dedications for the parents of seven generations of the donor's family and to enter meditation, and only then to receive the offerings. … At that time the monk Maudgalyāyana and the great bodhisattvas of the assembly all rejoiced greatly, and Maudgalyāyana's sorrowful weeping stopped as if washed away. That very day his mother was freed from a kalpa of suffering as a hungry ghost.
ur06.commentary: Monastics first making dedications for the donor's ancestors before receiving offerings continues today in the form of the Baekjung memorial ceremony. The story comes to a close as Maudgalyāyana's weeping stops.

ur07.heading: Devoted Children of Later Ages Too
ur07.plain: Maudgalyāyana again asked the Buddha: "The mother who bore me has received the merit of the Three Jewels and the majestic power of the Sangha. In ages to come, if all children of the Buddha wish to practice filial devotion, can they too uphold this Ullambana and save present parents and parents of seven generations?" The Buddha said: "An excellent question indeed."
ur07.commentary: Maudgalyāyana does not stop at saving his own mother; he asks on behalf of all children of later ages. One person's devotion becomes a path for everyone.

ur08.heading: Remember Your Parents Every Year
ur08.plain: The Buddha said to the good men and good women: "Children of the Buddha who cultivate filial devotion should remember their parents in every thought, make offerings to them, and think even of parents of seven generations. Every year on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, with a devoted and loving heart, remember the parents who bore you and parents of seven generations, prepare the Ullambana and give it to the Buddha and the Sangha, to repay the kindness of the parents who raised and loved you. All children of the Buddha should uphold this practice." … Then the monk Maudgalyāyana and the fourfold assembly heard the Buddha's words, rejoiced, and put them into practice.
ur08.commentary: The sutra ends with "remember your parents in every thought." The true meaning of Ullambana is a heart that always thinks of one's parents, not just on the day of Baekjung.

maudgalyayana.definition: One of the Buddha's ten great disciples, called "foremost in spiritual powers." With Śāriputra, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples.

six-abhijna.definition: Six powers gained through practice: going anywhere, seeing anything (the heavenly eye), hearing anything (the heavenly ear), knowing others' minds, knowing past lives, and the ending of afflictions.

preta.definition: A being always tormented by hunger and thirst, said to be born from the karma of greed and stinginess in life.

pravarana.definition: The ceremony at the end of the three-month summer retreat (15th day of the 7th lunar month) when monastics invite one another to point out their faults freely and repent.

seven-generations.definition: Ancestors over seven generations; more broadly, all one's parents and ancestors over many lives.

three-paths.definition: The three paths of great suffering: hells, hungry ghosts and animals.

ullambana.definition: A word interpreted as "hanging upside down," referring to the offering made to rescue ancestors from such suffering. The Ullambana festival (Baekjung) on the 15th day of the 7th lunar month comes from it.

three-jewels.definition: The three treasures of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community of practitioners).
